## What it is

Congregational hymn accompaniment: soprano, alto, tenor and bass moving together, one chord per melody
note or two, each held until the next, no drums. The organ is the obvious instrument.

## A little history

Martin Luther's chorales (from the 1520s) gave Protestant congregations hymns to sing; J. S. Bach's
four-part harmonisations of them in his cantatas and passions (1720s-40s) became the model of how to
write harmony, and still are in theory classes. In England, Isaac Watts and Charles Wesley in the 1700s
wrote the texts; the collection *Hymns Ancient and Modern* (1861) and *The English Hymnal* (1906, music
edited by Ralph Vaughan Williams) set the four-part style of the Anglican hymnal. American hymnals, gospel
song and shape-note singing grew from the same roots.

## The band's version

- **Bass:** *Held roots*. **Comping:** *hymn*: three voices over the root. **Drums:** none.
- Choose Church organ as the instrument for the other obvious sound.

## Listening

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| J. S. Bach, *Wachet auf* chorale (Cantata 140, final movement) | 1731 | Four-part chorale. |
| Choir of King's College, Cambridge, *Once in Royal David's City* | any year | The hymn that opens their Christmas Eve service. |
| Vaughan Williams, *Down Ampney* (*Come Down, O Love Divine*) | 1906 | An English Hymnal tune. |
| Any congregational recording of *Old Hundredth* | 1551 tune | The oldest hymn tune still in common use. |

### More recent

| Recording | Year | Listen for |
|---|---|---|
| Keith Getty & Stuart Townend, *In Christ Alone* | 2001 | A modern hymn, often sung in four parts. |
| Chris Tomlin, *Amazing Grace (My Chains Are Gone)* | 2006 | An old hymn tune with a band. |
